title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
openingChapterLabel: Letter I — Walton to his Sister
openingText: You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings. I arrived here yesterday, and my first task is to assure my dear sister of my welfare and increasing confidence in the success of my undertaking.
about:
Frankenstein is the story of Victor Frankenstein, a young Genevan student at the University of Ingolstadt who learns the secret of imparting life to dead matter and assembles a creature from corpses. The being he wakes up is eight feet tall, intelligent, and hideous. Victor flees the laboratory in horror. The creature, abandoned, learns language by hiding in a hovel and watching a poor French family read aloud; he finds Victor's journal in a coat pocket and reads how he was made. He demands one thing — a female companion of his own kind — and when Victor refuses he begins killing the people Victor loves. The novel ends in the Arctic, where Victor has chased the creature across frozen sea and dies aboard the ship of an explorer named Walton.

Mary Shelley was eighteen when she began the book in the summer of 1816, on the shore of Lake Geneva, during the "year without a summer." She had eloped two years earlier with Percy Shelley; their first child had died at eleven days old. Byron, who was renting the Villa Diodati nearby, proposed that each of them write a ghost story. Hers became Frankenstein. She finished it at twenty; it was published anonymously in three volumes in 1818, with a preface by Percy that some readers assumed meant he had written it. The novel is structured as nested narratives — Walton's letters to his sister enclose Victor's confession, which encloses the creature's own account of his life — three tellings of the same calamity from progressively further inside it.

It is the founding text of science fiction and one of the founding texts of modern horror, but it is not really a horror novel. It is a serious moral argument, written by a teenage mother, about what creators owe what they have made.

angleCards.title: The creature as the moral centre.
angleCards.text: The creature's argument against Frankenstein — I did not ask to exist, you made me, you abandoned me — is the most coherent position in the novel. I want to read it asking whether Victor ever genuinely engages with it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Frankenstein with the creature as the moral centre — I want to follow his argument against Frankenstein, which I believe is the strongest argument in the novel, and understand what it means that Victor never answers it.

angleCards.title: The responsibility of creators.
angleCards.text: Frankenstein brings a conscious being into existence and then flees from it. I want to think through what he owed the creature he made — and what the novel proposes about the ethics of creation.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Frankenstein to think about the responsibility of creators — what Frankenstein owes the being he made, whether he ever fulfils that obligation, and what the novel proposes about the ethics of bringing a new being into existence.

angleCards.title: Shelley writing about ambition.
angleCards.text: Mary Shelley was 19 when she began this novel. Her mother died giving birth to her. Her own child died. I want to read Frankenstein knowing who wrote it and why the question of bringing life into being mattered so personally.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Frankenstein as a 19-year-old's warning about what happens when men pursue knowledge and creation without thinking about consequences — and I want to understand what Shelley, writing from her own experience, was working through.

angleCards.title: Horror or loneliness?
angleCards.text: The monster of popular culture is nothing like Shelley's creature — who reads Milton, learns French, and desperately wants friendship. I want to read this as a novel about loneliness and ask whether that is more frightening than any monster.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Frankenstein asking whether this is really a horror novel or a novel about loneliness — about what it means to be created without being wanted, to be intelligent without being recognised, to exist without belonging.

cast.name: Victor Frankenstein
cast.description: A Genevan natural philosopher in his early twenties, brilliant, obsessive, and physically frail. He spends two years assembling and animating a being in a rented attic in Ingolstadt, then runs from the room the moment it opens its eyes. He spends the rest of the novel sick and pursued — by guilt, by the consequences of his cowardice, and finally by the creature itself across the Alps and into the Arctic. He never quite admits, even on his deathbed, that the violence he survived was caused by his own desertion.

cast.name: The Creature
cast.description: Eight feet tall, sewn from corpses, abandoned at the moment of his birth. He hides in a shed adjoining the De Lacey cottage for over a year, learning French and human kindness by watching them through a chink in the wall. He educates himself on Paradise Lost, Plutarch's Lives, and The Sorrows of Young Werther. He is gentle until rejection breaks him. His central chapters of self-narration, in which he describes how he became a murderer, are the most morally serious passages in the book.

cast.name: Robert Walton
cast.description: An English explorer leading a ship through the Arctic ice in pursuit of a polar passage. His letters to his sister Margaret open and close the novel. He finds Victor exhausted on a sledge, takes him aboard, hears his story, and at the end faces the choice of whether to push his crew further into danger for the sake of glory. Walton is no incidental frame: his ambition mirrors Victor's, and the novel rests on whether he learns the lesson Victor refused.

cast.name: Elizabeth Lavenza
cast.description: Victor's adopted cousin, raised in the Frankenstein household and engaged to him from childhood. She is patient, intelligent, devoted to a fiancé who keeps disappearing into laboratories and illnesses he will not explain. The creature warns Victor explicitly that he will be present on Victor's wedding night. Victor assumes the threat is to himself and arms himself accordingly. He guesses wrong. Her death is the most damning indictment of his refusal to take responsibility for what he made.

cast.name: Henry Clerval
cast.role: The Friend Victor Could Not See
cast.description: Victor's closest friend from boyhood, warm, literary, drawn to languages and people rather than chemistry. He travels to Ingolstadt to find Victor in a state of collapse and nurses him back to health for months. He travels with Victor across England and Scotland on the way to Victor's secret laboratory in the Orkneys. He has no idea what Victor is doing. The creature kills him while Victor is occupied elsewhere. Henry is the warmth Victor passed up for ambition, and his end is the novel's most bitter irony.

cast.name: The De Lacey Family
cast.description: An exiled French family — old blind Monsieur De Lacey, his son Felix, daughter Agatha, and Felix's Arabian fiancée Safie — living in poverty in a German cottage. The creature watches them through a wall for the better part of a year and learns language from the lessons Felix gives Safie. He helps them anonymously by gathering wood at night. When he finally introduces himself to the blind father, who treats him kindly, the sighted children return and attack him. Their rejection is the moment the creature decides on revenge.

acclaim.quote: It is no slight merit in our eyes, that the tale, though wild in incident, is written in plain and forcible English, without exhibiting that mixture of hyperbolical Germanisms with which tales of wonder are usually told.
acclaim.context: review in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, March 1818

whyItMatters.title: What Creators Owe What They Make
whyItMatters.body: Frankenstein is, before anything else, an argument about responsibility for what one has called into existence. Victor spends two years working in obsessive secrecy to give a body life; the moment that body opens its yellow eyes, he flees. He goes home, falls ill, and pretends the project never happened. The creature, alone, learns language, learns kindness, learns who made him, and comes back to ask what he is owed. "I ought to be thy Adam," he tells Victor, "but I am rather the fallen angel." The novel takes that grievance with full seriousness. Mary Shelley is not asking whether it is wise to create — she is asking what one owes the being one has created, whether or not it turned out as one hoped. The argument runs intact through every story now told about technologies that produce things their inventors did not foresee and cannot quite face.

whyItMatters.title: Two Voices, Equal Weight
whyItMatters.body: The novel's structure is its argument. Walton's letters frame Victor's confession; Victor's confession encloses, at its center, the creature's own narration of his year by the De Lacey cottage and his slow recognition of what he is. Shelley gives the creature about a hundred pages to describe his side. He is articulate, well-read, exact about how rejection turned him into a killer. By the end of his chapters most readers have moved fully into his point of view — and then Victor resumes the telling and tries, unsuccessfully, to recover the moral high ground. Few novels before Frankenstein had been willing to give the antagonist that much narrative space. The decision shapes everything that follows in fiction about monsters and outsiders. The creature is allowed to make his case in his own words, and the novel will not let any reader pretend not to have heard it.

whyItMatters.title: Science Reaching Into What Religion Held
whyItMatters.body: Shelley wrote at the precise hinge of the early industrial nineteenth century, when chemistry, physiology, and electricity were beginning to reach into territory religion had previously administered alone — life, death, the soul. Galvani had made dead frogs' legs twitch with current; Erasmus Darwin had speculated about spontaneous generation; the public had begun attending lectures on "animal electricity" as evening entertainment. Victor's experiment is fanciful, but the cultural anxiety the novel is metabolizing was not. The book does not reject science. Walton is allowed his ambition; Victor is granted his genius; the creature himself is, in part, an argument that what has been made is real and cannot be wished away. What the novel asks is what it means when humans do what gods used to do — and what they owe the new things they make. Two centuries later, the question has only sharpened around every laboratory that produces things its makers cannot quite control.
